Then the random SVM cluster was proposed to distinguish TC and ASD. The results show that this method has an excellent classiﬁcation performance based on all the features. Furthermore, the accuracy based on the optimal feature set could reach to 96.15%. Abnormal brain regions could also be found, such as inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) (orbital and opercula part), hippocampus, and precuneus. It is indicated that the method of random SVM cluster may apply to the auxiliary diagnosis of ASD. Keywords: random support vector machine cluster, neuroimaging, autism spectrum disorder, classiﬁcation, feature selection INTRODUCTION Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is mainly reﬂected in the communication and language barriers, diﬃculties in social communication, and it is a kind of neurological developmental disorder (Karten and Hirsch, 2015; Khundrakpam et al., 2017). The behavioral phenotype of ASD is well-depicted but its etiology and pathogenesis is rarely known (Amaral et al., 2008). According to the results of Hallmayer et al. (2011), the causes of ASD mainly include genetic and environmental risk factors. Some of the symptoms of ASD generally appear in about 2 years old (Ecker et al., 2015), thus the early diagnosis is needed (Plitt et al., 2015). It is recognized that traditional clinical methods cannot well distinguish patients from healthy controls (HC) (Mwangi et al., 2012). And it may not be complex enough to capture the abnormal brain regions in individuals who suﬀering from ASD (Uddin et al., 2011). To avoid this disadvantage, machine learning is introduced in the neuroimaging ﬁeld. It is a valid means to extract messages from neuroimaging data and further predict the future changes of the disease (Klöppel et al., 2012; Orrù et al., 2012). Among numerous machine learning methods, support vector machines (SVM) is an excellent classiﬁcation method Bi et al. Classiﬁcation of ASD Using Random-SVM-Cluster (Zhang et al., 2015). SVM has distinct merits such as the higher classiﬁcation accuracy (Zhang and Wu, 2012) and no need for a large number of training samples to avoid over-ﬁtting (Li et al., 2010). Thus, SVM has aroused widespread concern of researchers in the ﬁeld of neuroimaging (Sundermann et al., 2014). In the researches of machine learning, SVM has been applied to classify ASD from corresponding controls. Gori et al. (2015) extracted features from the gray matter subregions, then these features were used in SVM to identity ASD from HC and the area under ROC curve (AUC) is 0.74. Jin et al. (2015) proposed an original multi-kernel SVM classiﬁcation method to classify ASD from HC and the accuracy can reach to 76%. Chen et al. (2016) used the SVM to classify 112 adolescent subjects with ASD and 128 HC, and the classiﬁcation accuracy was 79.17%. Odriozola et al. (2015) used the SVM based on functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data to classify 20 children with ASD and 20 typically developing (TD) peers, and the result showed 85% classiﬁcation accuracy. Chanel et al. (2016) used the method of SVM and Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) based on fMRI data to classify ASD from HC, and the result showed good classiﬁcation accuracy (up to 92.3%). These SVM classiﬁcation studies on ASD have achieved relatively high classiﬁcation accuracy in the range of 70–93% compared with traditional methods. They usually employed a single SVM and common features such as functional connections, gray matter volume to classify ASD from HC, and the classiﬁcation accuracy is generally lower than 90%. In this paper, a novel method of random SVM cluster is proposed and several graph metrics of brain functional connectivity (e.g., local eﬃciency, shortest path) are employed to classify ASD and typical controls (TC). This method has some good performance. Firstly, the classiﬁcation accuracy reaches to a higher level based on all the features. Then, we could ﬁnd out the optimal feature set, the classiﬁcation accuracy could also reach to the same level based on the optimal feature set. Thirdly, on the basis of the optimal feature set, we could ﬁnd out the abnormal brain regions such as inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) (orbital and opercula part), hippocampus, and precuneus. Thus, the random SVM cluster may apply to the auxiliary diagnosis of ASD. MATERIALS AND METHODS Demographic Information The Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE) database (http://fcon_1000.projects.nitrc.org/indi/abide/) (Di Martino et al., 2014) contains a variety of neuroimaging data. And the resting-state fMRI data include 539 ASD and 573 age-matched TC. There are 12 kinds of image protocols. This study chooses one of the image protocols, details as follows. MRI scanner = 3.0- T Siemens, TR = 3,000 ms, TE = 28 ms, data matrix = 64∗64, Pixel Spacing X = 3.0 mm, Pixel Spacing Y = 3.0 mm, Flip Angle = 90◦, Slice Thickness = 0.0 mm, no slice gap, axial slices = 34, time points = 120. Finally, 61 subjects with ASD and 46 TC met the image protocol. The original studies included in ABIDE received approval from each site’s Institutional Review Board (IRB). All images were obtained with informed consent according to procedures established by human subject research boards. Only 84 of 107 subjects are utilized in experiments because the translation or the rotation of 7 TC and 16 ASD patients has surpassed ± 2 mm or ± 2◦.

evidence_spans.text: fMRI image could be divided into 90 regions based on the Automatic Anatomical Labeling (AAL) (Tzourio-Mazoyer et al., 2002) atlas. We make these regions as the nodes of brain network, so there are 90 nodes. An average of the time series of a region’s all voxels can be used to capture the mean time series of this region (Khazaee et al., 2016). The average time series of every two brain regions can be employed to calculate the Pearson correlation coeﬃcient which is made as the link of the brain network (Khazaee et al., 2015), so there are 4,005 (90∗89/2) weighted edges.

The width argument of RBF equals to 3, and penalty coeﬃcient equals to Inf. The process is repeated for 500 times and these 500 SVMs constitute into a random SVM cluster.

evidence_spans.text: The overall best performing model was the MM-ensemble, which achieved balanced accuracy of 64% and F1 score of 66%, averaged over the ﬁve-folds of the CV procedure. evidence_spans.text: In this study, we used the fMRI data of 816 individuals enrolled in the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE) to introduce a new biomarker extraction pipeline for ASD that relies on the use of graph theoretical metrics of fMRI-based functional connectivity to inform a support vector machine (SVM).
evidence_spans.paper_title: Topological Properties of Resting-State fMRI Functional Networks Improve Machine Learning-Based Autism Classification
evidence_spans.claim: The study used fMRI data of 816 ABIDE individuals, extracting graph-theoretical metrics of functional connectivity to inform an SVM classifier.

evidence_spans.text: Our methodology achieved better results than most state-of-the-art investigations on this dataset with the best model for the >30 years age group achieving an accuracy, sensitivity, and speciﬁcity of 95, 97, and 95%, respectively.
evidence_spans.paper_title: Topological Properties of Resting-State fMRI Functional Networks Improve Machine Learning-Based Autism Classification
evidence_spans.claim: The best model (>30 years age group) achieved 95% accuracy, 97% sensitivity and 95% specificity.

evidence_spans.text: We minimized the risk of overﬁtting by using three limiting approaches. First, the simplest kernel (linear) was used for the SVM. synthesis_text:
Computed by `phase3/s4_synthesis.py` from the charted records (quotes re-verified against each paper's full text). Counts are papers; only charted values are counted, and 'not reported' is reported. The corpus is the 99 open-access papers retrieved from 200 sought (see `out/review.md` for the PRISMA flow); this is a second-pass eligibility assessment over those reports, not a census of ABIDE papers.

#### In brief

- 74 of 99 papers analysed ABIDE resting-state data; 25 were excluded, almost all (21) because they used only structural or phenotypic ABIDE data.
- Most work is on ABIDE I alone (54 papers); 16 combine I and II; 4 use II alone.
- Prediction dominates: 46 predictive, 7 predictive plus group difference, 20 group difference only.
- Of 53 predictive papers, 26 use cross-validation that mixes sites in train and test folds; only 6 hold whole sites out. Median best accuracy is 73.3% under pooled CV (23 papers; 70.9% without the leakage-flagged ones) and 66.8% under leave-site-out (5 papers). These are different papers, models and subsets, so the gap is descriptive, not a controlled comparison. Two papers report both schemes with numbers for the same model: S-030 drops from 64% to 56% balanced accuracy when sites are held out; S-072 reports about 60% pooled and 62% leave-site-out.
- 8 predictive papers are flagged for leakage (feature selection, harmonisation or tuning using data outside the training folds).
- The analysed cohort can be rebuilt exactly for 17 papers (a published participant list for only 4), partly for 42, not at all for 15.
- The most reused subset is ABIDE I N = 871 (403 ASD / 468 TD): 9 papers, including Abraham et al. (S-002; NeuroImage 2017, corpus year 2016), Parisot et al. 2018 (S-019) and Ktena et al. 2017 (S-024).
- Leave-site-out also appears as a robustness check for group differences (S-005, S-009), which is why the site-handling table counts 8 papers with leave-site-out against 6 in the evaluation table.

#### Who got in

- Assessed for eligibility: **99**; included **74**, excluded **25**.
- Read in full text: 98; on abstract only: 1 (S-040 — the retrieved PDF is a different paper).

- Exclusion 3: structural/DTI/phenotype-only ABIDE use (no resting-state analysis): 21
- Exclusion 4: ABIDE used only for methods benchmarking, no autism-vs-control analysis: 4

#### Which release, which kind of claim

| ABIDE release | papers |
|---|---|
| ABIDE I | 54 |
| ABIDE I+II | 16 |
| ABIDE II | 4 |

| Main claim | papers |
|---|---|
| predictive | 46 |
| associational | 20 |
| both | 7 |
| descriptor | 1 |

Analysed sample size (total N, 71 papers reporting it): median 871, range 27–2226; 2 did not report a total.

#### How prediction papers were evaluated

53 papers make a predictive claim (predictive only, or predictive plus a group difference). A paper can use more than one scheme.

bias_assessment: Predictive papers (n=53) were appraised with PROBAST domains (Participants, Predictors, Outcome, Analysis); overall: High 24, Low 19, Unclear 10. The Analysis domain drove most High ratings (25 High): single train/test splits without uncertainty, cross-validation pooling sites, and in 8 papers leakage — feature selection, harmonisation or tuning on data outside the training folds (S-011, S-014, S-016, S-027, S-052, S-060, S-077, S-099). Group-difference papers and the data descriptor (n=21) were appraised with JBI analytical cross-sectional items; overall: Low 15, Unclear 6. The commonest weaknesses were unreported motion/QC thresholds (CL2), no site handling (28 of 73 analysis papers), and cohorts that cannot be rebuilt from released files (RQ6 no: 15).
limitations: Corpus: 200 of 412 open-access primary records were sought (top by citation count, with quotas) and 99 retrieved; 101 were not retrieved (47 no OA PDF location known; 23 publisher OA URL served a bot-check page; 49 of the misses had a PMCID but PMC routes were blocked on 2026-10-15), including the ABIDE I descriptor (Di Martino 2014). Paywalled work is absent by design. Full texts were extracted with PyMuPDF; tables may be garbled. One retrieved PDF (S-040, 10.1016/j.biopsych.2017.09.029) is a different paper, so that record was assessed on its abstract. Screening, charting and appraisal were done by AI charting agents (Claude Sonnet, 8 batches), single-charted, without human double extraction; every quote was mechanically re-verified against the full text (1743 checked, 8 dropped, all empty strings), but the judgments themselves were not independently re-rated. Evaluation-scheme, headline-accuracy and site-handling categories were assigned by the merge agent from charted text, each tied to a verbatim charted snippet. Accuracies are not comparable across papers (different subsets, pipelines, models, metrics), so the scheme-wise distributions are descriptive. Shared cohorts are inferred from identical stated N and release, not from participant lists.

Diagnostic classification of autism vs t.outcome: Diagnostic classification of autism vs typical development from ABIDE rs-fMRI

Inconsistency.explanation: Headline accuracies span 58.0–96.91% under pooled CV alone.

Indirectness.explanation: 26 of 53 papers mix sites across folds; only 6 hold out whole sites, the setting closest to use on new scanners.

Imprecision.explanation: Most papers report point estimates; few give intervals.

Publication bias.explanation: Not assessable from this corpus (open-access, citation-ranked).

Diagnostic classification of autism vs t.summary: Very low certainty that the reported accuracies would hold on data from unseen sites.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Population heterogeneity in clinical cohorts affects the predictive accuracy of brain imaging
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Oualid Benkarim; Casey Paquola; Bo-yong Park; et al.
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Effect of population heterogeneity/diversity on predictive accuracy and pattern stability
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Quantify how demographic/site diversity (via propensity scores) affects cross-validated prediction accuracy and biomarker pattern stability in ASD classification
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: Multi-site (4 ABIDE sites: NYU, PITT, USM, TCD)
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: ADOS and/or ADI-R gold-standard diagnostics via in-person interview by board-certified mental health professionals
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 151 (297 total before matching); 145 after propensity-score matching
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Excluded: genetic disorders associated with autism (e.g. Fragile X), MRI contraindications, current pregnancy
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 146 (297 total before matching); 145 after propensity-score matching
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: true (propensity-score matched on age, sex, site)
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Yes — all imaging features, phenotypic data and analysis code openly available at https://github.com/OualidBenkarim/ps_diversity; figure data in S1 Data
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Region-to-region functional connectivity using a 100-region Schaefer-Yeo cortical parcellation atlas
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: C-PAC (Preprocessed Connectomes Project pipeline: slice-time correction, motion correction, skull stripping, intensity normalization, CompCor, band-pass filtering 0.01-0.1 Hz); FreeSurfer for structural/cortical thickness
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Model coefficient (weight vector) consistency via Pearson correlation across resampled models
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Linear classifier (predictive modeling of ASD vs TD from functional connectivity)
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Propensity-score-based stratified train/holdout partitioning (contiguous, diverse, random sampling schemes) with 10-fold CV within training strata; out-of-distribution evaluation on held-out strata
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: ABIDE: prediction performance declined as diversity increased — within-distribution AUC r=-0.630, F1 r=-0.568; out-of-distribution AUC r=-0.671, F1 r=-0.579. Deconfounding (linear regression r=-0.539; ComBat r=-0.599) only slightly reduced this correlation versus raw data (r=-0.671).
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: In ABIDE (and oppositely in HBN), predictive accuracy and pattern stability for ASD vs TD classification decline substantially as population diversity (quantified via propensity scores on age, sex, site) increases, and this effect persists after standard deconfounding (linear regression or ComBat), which were themselves computed using all participants rather than training data only.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Important methodological finding: propensity-score and deconfounding computations used the full dataset (not train-only), a leakage concern the authors themselves report.

data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Identify and validate cortical regions showing differential (cerebellar) functional connectivity between ASD and TD

data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: ASD showed reduced cortico-cerebellar functional connectivity with five cortical ROIs in the ABIDE I discovery sample (N=708); three of the five (right fusiform gyrus, right superior temporal gyrus, left middle temporal gyrus) replicated in an independent ABIDE II validation sample (N=585, 11 sites), all FDR-corrected.

data_charting_rubrics.title: MADE-for-ASD: A multi-atlas deep ensemble network for diagnosing Autism Spectrum Disorder
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Xuehan Liu; Md Rakibul Hasan; et al.
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Diagnose ASD vs typical controls from ABIDE I rs-fMRI functional connectivity plus demographic data using a weighted deep ensemble network
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: resting-state fMRI, demographic data (age, sex, handedness, FIQ)
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Code and evaluations publicly available at https://github.com/hasan-rakibul/MADE-for-ASD
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Functional connectivity matrices from AAL (116 ROIs), Craddock 200 (CC), and Eickhoff-Zilles (EZ) atlases; top features selected via F-score
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: CPAC pipeline (Preprocessed Connectomes Project)
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: F-score ranking
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Top 10 ROIs via F-score, e.g. precuneus and anterior cingulate/ventromedial prefrontal cortex
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Deep ensemble (stacked sparse denoising autoencoder + MLP, weighted voting)
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: SSDAE+MLP ensemble (MADE-for-ASD)
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: 10-fold cross-validation; evaluated on whole ABIDE I CPAC dataset, a data-selector-defined 'proposed subset', and the NYU site subset
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Whole dataset (N=1035): 75.20% accuracy, 82.90% sensitivity, 69.70% specificity. Proposed subset (N=645): 88.71% accuracy. NYU subset (N=175): 96.40% accuracy, 91.00% sensitivity, 99.50% specificity.
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: MADE-for-ASD achieves 75.20% accuracy on the whole ABIDE I CPAC dataset (N=1035), a 4.4-percentage-point improvement over prior SOTA on the same data, with higher accuracy (88.71%, 96.40%) on a self-selected 'proposed subset' and the NYU site subset respectively; demographic information and multi-atlas fusion are reported to improve performance.
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Improve interpretation of fMRI-derived features relative to autism symptoms; extend interpretability and clinical correlation of deep learning outputs.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The 'proposed subset' (645/1035, 88.71% accuracy) is defined as samples a pretrained selector model itself classified correctly — this is a circularity/leakage concern when reporting that subset's accuracy as a performance result.

custom_fields.RQ1: predictive — ABIDE I only, raw N=1112 reduced to 1,035 after preprocessing/QC (505 ASD, 530 TC); no explicit FD/motion threshold given in the extracted main text (QC described generically as reducing N to 1035, consistent with prior studies) | quote: "Although Di Martino et al. [11] released the ABIDE I dataset with 1,112 samples, prepro- cessing and quality control reduced this number to 1,035"
custom_fields.RQ2: CPAC pipeline (one of four Preprocessed Connectomes Project pipelines); three atlases: AAL (116 ROIs), Craddock 200 (CC), Eickhoff-Zilles (EZ) | quote: "We, therefore, leverage the CPAC pipeline, hereinafter referred to as the ABIDE I CPAC data."
custom_fields.RQ3: predictive — ASD vs TC diagnostic classification using a weighted deep ensemble network | quote: "We use rs-fMRI and demographic data from ABIDE I [11], the first phase of ABIDE, with 505 autistic individuals and 530 Typical Controls (TCs)."

data_charting_rubrics.title: Promises, Pitfalls, and Basic Guidelines for Applying Machine Learning Classifiers to Psychiatric Imaging Data, with Autism as an Example
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Kassraian-Fard et al.
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Diagnosis / methodological tutorial on ML classification pitfalls
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Demonstrate and compare ML classification pipelines for ASD vs TD using ABIDE RS-fMRI data, while teaching methodological pitfalls (peeking/double-dipping, site effects)
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: MATLAB code for all pipelines publicly available (ETH website)
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: 200x200 Craddock-atlas ROI-to-ROI Pearson correlation matrix (19,900 features)
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: SPM12 (realignment, DARTEL normalization, smoothing, band-pass filter 0.01-0.05Hz, motion scrubbing)
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Mean-difference threshold feature selection (t-value threshold), with nested CV for threshold tuning
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Multiple classical ML classifiers compared
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Logistic regression, lasso-regularized logistic regression, linear SVM, probabilistic neural network, linear discriminant analysis, Gaussian naive Bayes
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Nested 10x10-fold cross-validation (outer loop for performance, inner loop for feature-selection/tuning-parameter selection); explicit avoidance of double-dipping via train-only feature selection and standardization
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: LR 58%, LassoLR 58%, SVM 63% (best out-of-the-box), PNN 58%, LDA 57%, GNB 61% accuracy; SVM accuracy increased to 68% after per-site (train-only) z-standardization; all classifiers significantly better than chance (p<0.001).
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Out-of-the-box ML classifiers applied correctly (nested CV) to ABIDE rs-fMRI connectivity achieve about 60-70% accuracy (best: SVM 63%, improving to 68% with site standardization); incorrect feature selection on the full dataset ('peeking'/double-dipping) can spuriously inflate accuracy to 91% in a null simulation, illustrating a major pitfall in the field.
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Leave-one-site-out cross-validation and further site-effect correction beyond linear z-transformation; stable feature selection methods for biomarker interpretation.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: A methods/tutorial paper that nonetheless performs an original classification analysis on real ABIDE data; valuable as a positive worked example of leakage-avoidance practice for the review's CL5 checklist item.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Using Functional or Structural Magnetic Resonance Images and Personal Characteristic Data to Identify ADHD and Autism
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Sina Ghiassian; Russell Greiner; Ping Jin; Matthew Brown
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Build a single automated learning pipeline (MHPC) to classify ADHD (ADHD-200) and autism (ABIDE) from functional/structural MRI and personal characteristic data
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: Multi-site (17 institutions, North America and Europe)
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: resting-state fMRI, structural MRI, personal characteristic data (age, sex, handedness, IQ measures, site, eye status)
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Yes — ABIDE and ADHD-200 datasets are both publicly available online; no separate analysis code repository mentioned
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Voxel-based image texture (3D Histogram of Oriented Gradients) + personal characteristic data
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: 3D-HOG features extracted from functional or structural MRI (no ROI/atlas parcellation); feature selection via minimum-redundancy-maximum-relevance (MRMR)
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: SPM8 + in-house MATLAB preprocessing pipeline (motion correction, co-registration, spatial normalization to MNI)
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: MRMR feature selection; features mapped back to brain regions
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Ensemble of classical ML base learners (MHPC system)
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Linear SVM, RBF-kernel SVM, decision trees, k-nearest neighbours, naive Bayes

data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: ABIDE hold-out: Functional MRI 59.2% (baseline 51.6%), Structural MRI 60.1%, Personal Characteristic 59.6%, Structural+PCD 64.1%, Functional+PCD 65.0% (best) accuracy.
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Combining resting-state fMRI-derived HOG features with personal characteristic data achieved the best ABIDE hold-out accuracy of 65.0% (baseline 51.6%), outperforming functional MRI alone (59.2%), structural MRI alone (60.1%), and PCD alone (59.6%), and outperforming the then-best published ABIDE result (60.0% over a 53.6% baseline).
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Site of imaging is used as an input feature rather than harmonised away or held out, which may let the classifier partly learn site identity rather than purely disorder-related signal.

data_charting_rubrics.authors: Lee et al.
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Examine whether ASD functional under-connectivity originates from ipsilateral or contralateral (inter-hemispheric) brain regions using whole-brain voxel-wise FCD mapping
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: Multi-site (subset of ABIDE I sites contributing both ASD and TDC)

data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Hypoconnectivity: decreased inter- and intra-hemispheric FCD in ASD vs TDC in posterior cingulate cortex, lingual/parahippocampal gyrus, and postcentral gyrus
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Voxel-wise 2-tailed t-test (age, sex covariates), FDR-corrected P<0.05, minimum cluster size 20 voxels; Benjamini-Hochberg correction for clinical-correlation analyses
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: ASD showed significantly decreased inter- and intra-hemispheric functional connectivity density relative to TDC in the posterior cingulate cortex, lingual/parahippocampal gyrus, and postcentral gyrus; ADOS-RRB (restricted/repetitive behavior) scores correlated negatively with FCD in these regions, including the default mode network.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Posterior cingulate cortex, lingual/parahippocampal gyrus, postcentral gyrus (decreased inter- and intra-hemispheric FCD in ASD)
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: No motion-based subject exclusion threshold or site covariate/harmonisation reported, despite pooling 15 ABIDE sites; age and sex only used as covariates.

It is indicated that the method of random SVM cluster may apply to the auxiliary diagnosis of ASD. Keywords: random support vector machine cluster, neuroimaging, autism spectrum disorder, classiﬁcation, feature selection INTRODUCTION Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is mainly reﬂected in the communication and language barriers, diﬃculties in social communication, and it is a kind of neurological developmental disorder (Karten and Hirsch, 2015; Khundrakpam et al., 2017). The behavioral phenotype of ASD is well-depicted but its etiology and pathogenesis is rarely known (Amaral et al., 2008). According to the results of Hallmayer et al. (2011), the causes of ASD mainly include genetic and environmental risk factors. Some of the symptoms of ASD generally appear in about 2 years old (Ecker et al., 2015), thus the early diagnosis is needed (Plitt et al., 2015). It is recognized that traditional clinical methods cannot well distinguish patients from healthy controls (HC) (Mwangi et al., 2012). And it may not be complex enough to capture the abnormal brain regions in individuals who suﬀering from ASD (Uddin et al., 2011). To avoid this disadvantage, machine learning is introduced in the neuroimaging ﬁeld. It is a valid means to extract messages from neuroimaging data and further predict the future changes of the disease (Klöppel et al., 2012; Orrù et al., 2012). Among numerous machine learning methods, support vector machines (SVM) is an excellent classiﬁcation method Bi et al. Classiﬁcation of ASD Using Random-SVM-Cluster (Zhang et al., 2015). SVM has distinct merits such as the higher classiﬁcation accuracy (Zhang and Wu, 2012) and no need for a large number of training samples to avoid over-ﬁtting (Li et al., 2010). Thus, SVM has aroused widespread concern of researchers in the ﬁeld of neuroimaging (Sundermann et al., 2014). In the researches of machine learning, SVM has been applied to classify ASD from corresponding controls. Gori et al. (2015) extracted features from the gray matter subregions, then these features were used in SVM to identity ASD from HC and the area under ROC curve (AUC) is 0.74. Jin et al. (2015) proposed an original multi-kernel SVM classiﬁcation method to classify ASD from HC and the accuracy can reach to 76%. Chen et al. (2016) used the SVM to classify 112 adolescent subjects with ASD and 128 HC, and the classiﬁcation accuracy was 79.17%. Odriozola et al. (2015) used the SVM based on functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data to classify 20 children with ASD and 20 typically developing (TD) peers, and the result showed 85% classiﬁcation accuracy. Chanel et al. (2016) used the method of SVM and Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) based on fMRI data to classify ASD from HC, and the result showed good classiﬁcation accuracy (up to 92.3%). These SVM classiﬁcation studies on ASD have achieved relatively high classiﬁcation accuracy in the range of 70–93% compared with traditional methods. They usually employed a single SVM and common features such as functional connections, gray matter volume to classify ASD from HC, and the classiﬁcation accuracy is generally lower than 90%. In this paper, a novel method of random SVM cluster is proposed and several graph metrics of brain functional connectivity (e.g., local eﬃciency, shortest path) are employed to classify ASD and typical controls (TC). This method has some good performance. Firstly, the classiﬁcation accuracy reaches to a higher level based on all the features. Then, we could ﬁnd out the optimal feature set, the classiﬁcation accuracy could also reach to the same level based on the optimal feature set. Thirdly, on the basis of the optimal feature set, we could ﬁnd out the abnormal brain regions such as inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) (orbital and opercula part), hippocampus, and precuneus. Thus, the random SVM cluster may apply to the auxiliary diagnosis of ASD. MATERIALS AND METHODS Demographic Information The Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE) database (http://fcon_1000.projects.nitrc.org/indi/abide/) (Di Martino et al., 2014) contains a variety of neuroimaging data. And the resting-state fMRI data include 539 ASD and 573 age-matched TC. There are 12 kinds of image protocols. This study chooses one of the image protocols, details as follows. MRI scanner = 3.0- T Siemens, TR = 3,000 ms, TE = 28 ms, data matrix = 64∗64, Pixel Spacing X = 3.0 mm, Pixel Spacing Y = 3.0 mm, Flip Angle = 90◦, Slice Thickness = 0.0 mm, no slice gap, axial slices = 34, time points = 120. Finally, 61 subjects with ASD and 46 TC met the image protocol. The original studies included in ABIDE received approval from each site’s Institutional Review Board (IRB). All images were obtained with informed consent according to procedures established by human subject research boards. Only 84 of 107 subjects are utilized in experiments because the translation or the rotation of 7 TC and 16 ASD patients has surpassed ± 2 mm or ± 2◦."

data_charting_rubrics.authors: Ibrahim Salim; A. Ben Hamza
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_diagnosis: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) vs healthy control (HC)
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: functional connectivity; phenotypic (gender, age, acquisition site used as graph edge weights)
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Fisher z-transformed Pearson correlation connectivity matrices over Harvard-Oxford atlas ROIs; recursive-feature-elimination-reduced upper-triangular connectivity vector; population graph edges weighted by gender, age and acquisition site
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: C-PAC (Configurable Pipeline for the Analysis of Connectomes); Harvard-Oxford atlas
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Graph convolutional network (population-graph node classification) with attention/skip-connection aggregation
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: AN-GCN (proposed), compared against Logistic Regression, Gradient Boosting, GCN, InceptionGCN, EV-GCN, LGL, HI-GCN, MMGL, DeepGCN, DS-MML

data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: AN-GCN: 96.91% accuracy, 96.86% AUC, 97.16% F1, 96.91% recall, 97.00% precision on ABIDE, versus the strongest baseline DS-MML (87.62% accuracy, 92.00% AUC) and baseline GCN (64.63% accuracy, 72.23% AUC); a relative improvement of 50.33% in accuracy over GCN
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: A population-graph GCN with skip connections and identity mapping (AN-GCN) classified ASD vs HC on 871 ABIDE subjects (403 ASD/468 HC) with 96.91% accuracy and 96.86% AUC, substantially exceeding all compared baselines including a strong recent method (DS-MML, 87.62% accuracy); feature reduction (recursive feature elimination) is described prior to the cross-validation step and site/age/gender are embedded directly as population-graph edge weights, raising a leakage/inflation concern given this result is far above both the paper's own baselines and typical published ABIDE benchmarks.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Reported 96.91% accuracy is markedly higher than the paper's own strongest baseline (87.62%) and most published ABIDE classification results, consistent with the leakage risk noted (feature elimination preceding CV; transductive population graph using site/age/gender from all subjects).

data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: A secondary 130-subject adult ABIDE I subsample (63 ASD, 67 NT, ages 18-50) was used only to assess generalization of the framework, not as the primary analysed cohort.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Hierarchical feature extraction on functional brain networks for autism spectrum disorder identification with resting-state fMRI data
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Yiqian Luo; Qiurong Chen; Fali Li; Yi Liang; Peng Xu; Yangsong Zhang

data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Lab-made pipeline based on FSL (FSL-BET, FSL-BBreg, FSL-FNIRT, CompCor, dual regression), noted as methodologically similar to C-PAC
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Dual-regression functional connectivity against the Smith et al. 2009 RSN10 resting-state network template (no discrete ROI atlas)
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Univariate biomarker / ROC analysis
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Two-sample t-test (FWE-corrected) for group differences; receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis of individual biomarkers
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Biomarkers derived from the full ABIDE I+II dataset, then independently validated (group difference, correlation, and ROC/AUC) on a separate local (KMUH) cohort
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: AUC (ROC analysis), Pearson correlation coefficients, FDR-adjusted p-values
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: DMN-derived biomarker A4 AUC = 0.745 (significantly higher than the RSN-template-only biomarker R4, AUC = 0.590, p<0.05) for distinguishing ASD in the local cohort
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Default mode network (DMN) and executive control network (ECN) biomarkers differed significantly between ASD and TD
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: DMN functional connectivity was weaker (hypoconnectivity) in ASD than TD; A4 (DMN) biomarker negatively correlated with SRS severity scores
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: The 30 biomarker masks and pipeline are shared on GitHub (https://github.com/htygithub/ASDmask/); the underlying datasets (including the local cohort) are available only from the corresponding author on reasonable request

both — derives group-difference biomarkers (ASD vs TD, FWE-corrected t-test) in ABIDE and evaluates their diagnostic utility (ROC/AUC) in an independent local cohort. | quote: "a receiver operating characteristic analysis to evaluate the classification performances of the 
biomarkers."
custom_fields.RQ4:
Two-sample t-tests with FWE correction (FSL-randomise, 5000 permutations) for ABIDE group differences; Pearson correlation with FDR-adjusted p-values and ROC/AUC analysis in the KMUH validation cohort; no site covariate or leave-site-out scheme for the pooled ABIDE derivation step. | quote: "FC val-
ues significantly different [family-wise error (FWE)-corrected p < 0.05] between the ASD and TD groups"

DMN functional connectivity was weaker in ASD than TD; DMN-derived biomarker A4 achieved AUC 0.745 in the local cohort (vs 0.590 for its RSN-template counterpart R4, p<0.05); DMN biomarkers correlated negatively with SRS severity. | quote: "The results of this study indicate that the FC of DMN in the ASD group was 
weaker than that of the TD group."

data_charting_rubrics.title: Alterations in Connectome Dynamics in Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Harmonized Mega- and Meta-analysis Study Using the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange Dataset
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Yapei Xie; Zhilei Xu; Mingrui Xia; Jin Liu; Xiao‐Jing Shou; Zaixu Cui; Xuhong Liao; Yong He
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Characterise ASD-vs-HC alterations in resting-state dynamic connectome modular structure and link them to social-impairment severity and gene expression.
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Resting-state (eyes open/closed as per site protocol, not further specified)
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: ABIDE site clinical diagnosis; ADOS-2 and ADI-R scores reported for characterization
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: 5-35 years (initial ABIDE range before age<35 restriction)
data_charting_rubrics.medications_therapies: Medicated ASD individuals were not excluded (limited medication information available from ABIDE)
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: No significant age difference between ASD and HC (p = .84)
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Modular variability of dynamic brain connectomes (512-node random parcellation, sliding-window multilayer network model)
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: GRETNA package
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Frequency of nodal selection as a feature during LOOCV
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Medial prefrontal cortex and visual cortex nodes made the largest contribution to SRS prediction
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Higher modular variability in ASD in default-mode regions (medial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate, angular gyrus); lower modular variability in ASD in visual cortex
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Support vector regression
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Support vector regression (LIBSVM) predicting SRS score from whole-brain modular variability maps
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) for SRS prediction; leave-one-site-out cross-validation as a sensitivity analysis for group differences
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Correlation (r) between predicted and actual SRS scores, permutation test
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: we found that brain dynamics was a significant predictor of SRS scores (r = .16, pperm = .002)
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: ASD showed higher mean and lower variance of whole-brain dynamic modular variability than HC, with regionally higher variability in default-mode regions and lower variability in visual cortex; modular variability predicted SRS social-impairment severity and correlated with ASD-risk gene expression patterns.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Dynamic modular variability in default-mode network regions (higher in ASD) and visual cortex (lower in ASD)
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Extend to female participants and other age ranges; incorporate ASD-specific (not only healthy) gene expression data when available.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Common and unique multimodal covarying patterns in autism spectrum disorder subtypes
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Shile Qi; Robin Morris; Jessica A. Turner; Zening Fu; Rongtao Jiang; Thomas P. DeRamus; Dongmei Zhi; Vince D. Calhoun; Jing Sui （Beijing Normal University）， my correct affiliation is beijing normal university, not Qingdao University of Science and Technology, please correct the current affiliation. Thank you
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Identify common and subtype-unique functional (fALFF) and structural (GM) covarying brain patterns among Asperger's, PDD-NOS and Autistic subgroups, and test their ability to predict ADOS/SRS symptom scores in an independent cohort.
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Multi-site (9 sites ABIDE II discovery; 17 sites ABIDE I replication)
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: most of the sites used the ADOS and Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised (ADI-R) scores to diagnose ASD
data_charting_rubrics.medications_therapies: Medication use of participants reported in Table 1
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: ADOS and SRS total/subdomain scores used as severity measures
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: The supervised fusion code has been released and integrated in the Fusion ICA Toolbox (FIT), which can be downloaded and used directly by users worldwide. The multimodal MRI data used in this study can be accessed upon application from ABIDE consortium.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: ABIDE data accessible upon application from the ABIDE consortium
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Voxel-wise fALFF (functional) and GM volume (structural) maps
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: fALFF and GM voxel maps fused via MCCAR+jICA guided by ADOS scores; no atlas/parcellation (voxel-wise analysis)
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: SPM12 (MATLAB 2019)
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Back-reconstruction of group differences and correlation of components with ADOS subdomains
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: DLPFC and superior/middle temporal cortex common across subtypes; subcortical regions unique per subtype (putamen-parahippocampus Asperger's, ACC PDD-NOS, thalamus-amygdala-caudate Autistic)
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: negative fALFF in anterior cingulate cortex unique to PDD-NOS subtype; and negative thalamus–amygdala–caudate fALFF unique to the Autistic subtype.
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Multivariate linear regression
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: MCCAR+jICA fusion (discovery) + multiple linear regression (cross-cohort symptom-score prediction)
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Discovery in ABIDE II, cross-cohort replication/prediction in independent ABIDE I sample; leave-one-site-out sensitivity analysis
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Correlation between predicted and true symptom scores; normalized root mean squared prediction error (NRMSE)
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: models can be generalized to predict ADOS and SRS scores for the corresponding subgroup from ABIDE I, but not for the other groups
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: DLPFC and superior/middle temporal cortex are shared functional-structural covarying areas across ASD subtypes; each subtype shows unique subcortical fALFF alterations correlated with distinct ADOS subdomains, and subtype-specific brain patterns predict symptom severity only within the matching subtype when generalized from ABIDE II to ABIDE I.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: negative fALFF in anterior cingulate cortex unique to PDD-NOS subtype; and negative thalamus–amygdala–caudate fALFF unique to the Autistic subtype.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Association between resting-state functional brain connectivity and gene expression is altered in autism spectrum disorder
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Stefano Berto; Alex Treacher; Emre Caglayan; Danni Luo; Jillian R. Haney; Michael J. Gandal; Daniel H. Geschwind; Albert Montillo; Geneviève Konopka
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Identify genes whose cortical expression is differentially correlated with resting-state brain activity (fALFF, ReHo) between ASD and control individuals.
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Multi-site (37 sites overall; 30 sites in the site-correction step)
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Individuals with Chromosome 15q Duplication were excluded from downstream gene-expression analysis
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: resting-state fMRI, post-mortem cortical RNA-seq gene expression
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Yes - code on GitHub; ABIDE imaging data available to approved investigators via NITRC/1000 Functional Connectomes registration
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: fALFF and ReHo averaged over an 11-region Brodmann-area atlas matched to RNA-seq regions
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: C-PAC v1.8.0
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Fisher r-to-z transformation of ASD vs CTL gene-fMRI correlations, combined via Fisher's method, FDR-corrected
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: FILIP1 and GABRQ among genes with highest effect size
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: 415 differentially correlated (DC) genes identified; 59.8% showed similarly-signed positive correlation with fALFF/ReHo in both groups
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: 415 genes were differentially correlated between ASD and controls with rs-fMRI activity (fALFF/ReHo) at Diff Cor P<0.01, CTL FDR<0.05, with effect sizes >1.8 for ~3% of expressed genes; these DC genes show altered postnatal developmental expression trajectories relevant to ASD.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Cortical regional fALFF/ReHo correlated with expression of 415 genes (including FILIP1, GABRQ) differently in ASD vs controls, especially in primary visual and inferior temporal cortex.

custom_fields.RQ1: ABIDE I+II across 37 sites (30 sites in the site-correction procedure), initial 916 ASD/1067 CTL (1983 total), QC'd to 710 ASD (79% male) / 606 CTL (87% male), ages 5-64 | quote: "After the removal of subjects with image artifacts, high head movement, or poor MNI152 coregistration, we analyzed the data from the remaining 710 ASD (79% male), and 606 CTL (87% male) subjects, whose age ranges from 5 to 64 years."
custom_fields.RQ2: C-PAC v1.8.0 pipeline; 11-region Brodmann-area atlas parcellation of fALFF and ReHo maps | quote: "The package CPAC v1.8.0 was used for fMRI pre-processing including head motion correction, scrubbing, and nuisance regression."
custom_fields.RQ3: associational — differential correlation between rs-fMRI measures (fALFF/ReHo) and gene expression, ASD vs controls | quote: "415 differentially corre- lated genes (DC genes; Diff Cor P < 0.01, CTL FDR < 0.05"
custom_fields.RQ4: Fisher r-to-z test of ASD vs CTL correlation differences, combined by Fisher's method, Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction; age/site/sex regressed out by linear model, site-mean correction applied | quote: "To reduce the impact of confounders, we regressed out age, site, and sex using a linear model."
custom_fields.RQ5: 415 differentially correlated genes identified (Diff Cor P<0.01, CTL FDR<0.05), effect size >1.8 for ~3% of expressed genes, with regional emphasis on primary visual and inferior temporal cortex | quote: "415 differentially corre- lated genes (DC genes; Diff Cor P < 0.01, CTL FDR < 0.05"

data_charting_rubrics.title: Deep learning based joint fusion approach to exploit anatomical and functional brain information in autism spectrum disorders
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Sara Saponaro; Francesca Lizzi; Giacomo Serra; Francesca Mainas; P. Oliva; Alessia Giuliano; Sara Calderoni; Alessandra Retico
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Classify ASD vs. TD using a deep-learning joint fusion of structural (Freesurfer) and functional (C-PAC) MRI features from ABIDE.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: To allow the reproducibility of the analysis, the identification numbers (IDs) of the participants selected in the final sample are reported in Additional file 1.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Structural morphometry (221 Freesurfer features) and functional connectivity (5253 Fisher-z FC features)
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Freesurfer aseg/aparc morphometric features (Desikan-Killiany-Tourville atlas) and pairwise Pearson functional connectivity (Harvard-Oxford atlas, 103 regions)
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Freesurfer v6.0 (recon-all) for structural; C-PAC for functional
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: SHAP (Gradient SHAP) applied within the inner CV loop, averaged over 100 folds; features above the 99th percentile selected as most important
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: brain changes tend to occur in individuals with ASD in regions belonging to the Default Mode Network and to the Social Brain.
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Deep learning (joint-fusion neural network)
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Feature-reduction neural network + classification neural network joint-fusion model, compared to single-modality (structural-only, functional-only) neural networks
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Nested 10-fold cross-validation (inner loop for training/feature scaling/SHAP, outer loop for performance evaluation); site harmonization (NeuroHarmonize/ComBat) performed on the full cohort prior to CV
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: AUC, accuracy (mean ± SD across outer folds)
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: The AUC values of 0.66±0.05 and of 0.76±0.04 were obtained in the ASD vs. TD discrimination when only structural or functional features are considered, respectively. The joint fusion approach led to an AUC of 0.78±0.04.
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: A multimodal deep-learning joint fusion of structural and functional MRI features (AUC 0.78±0.04) outperformed single-modality models (structural AUC 0.66±0.05; functional AUC 0.76±0.04) for ASD vs TD discrimination, with the most discriminative features localizing to the Default Mode Network and Social Brain regions.

custom_fields.CL6 Site handling reported (site covaria:
No — the combined-dataset analysis explicitly pools all 17 sites "ignoring the sites intrinsic variability"; no harmonisation or leave-site-out evaluation reported for this headline result (site-wise results are reported separately per site, not as leave-site-out). | quote: "ﬁrst the correlation-based connectivity matrix is arranged on all the sites,
ignoring the sites intrinsic variability, then a 10-fold cross-validation-based accuracy, sensitivity and
speciﬁcity is given in the mentioned table."
custom_fields.CL7 Code and/or participant list availab: No — no code repository or participant list link found in the text.
custom_fields.CL8 ABIDE relation of this paper: uses-d: uses-data

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Data descriptor; ABIDE II release; N=487 ASD, N=557 controls (1,044 datasets total) across 17 collections and 16 sites (9 ABIDE I charter sites + 7 new).
narrative_rows.methods: Describes data contribution, anonymization, and aggregation procedures across sites; diagnosis basis per collection (ADOS/ADI-R and/or clinical judgment); QC assessed with the Preprocessed Connectomes Project protocol (spatial and temporal metrics including mean FD) but not used to exclude data.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Cohort composition, demographic and phenotypic variable availability (SRS, RBS-R, ADOS/ADI-R), and QC metric distributions by collection are reported; no group-difference or classification analysis is performed.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: Heterogeneity across sites in inclusion/exclusion criteria, scanners and acquisition parameters; no consensus QC threshold is applied, so users must select/exclude data themselves.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Defines the ABIDE II release structure (collections, sites, Ns, diagnosis basis, QC metrics) that downstream analysis papers subset from; central for linking any ABIDE II-using publication to its data provenance.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Diagnostic prediction (CNN and transfer learning); ABIDE-I (1112 datasets: 539 ASD, 573 TC) and ABIDE-II (reported as 1114 or 1014 datasets: 521 ASD, 593 TC) across 17 sites; combined ABIDE-I+II analysis also reported.
narrative_rows.methods: MRI-derived images/heat maps from ABIDE rs-fMRI data are classified with an optimized CNN and a transfer-learning model (DTL-NN); results reported separately per data-collection site/resource and per age-based subgroup, with no described preprocessing pipeline, atlas, or train/test split.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and F1-score reported per site and per dataset grouping; best combined ABIDE-I+II result: CNN 81.56% accuracy, DTL-NN 82.31% accuracy.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: Authors note limitations from multi-site data collection (17 sites) and picture data availability (851 subjects); no cross-validation/held-out evaluation, no diagnosis-source documentation, no preprocessing/atlas details, inconsistent N reporting between abstract and tables.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Uses ABIDE I and II for diagnostic prediction but with minimal methodological transparency on cohort construction, QC, pipeline, and validation — illustrates reconstructibility and rigor gaps relevant to the dataset-publication link.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Group-difference (associational) seed-based connectivity study; primary cohort is the authors' own lab sample (23 ASD, 20 TD); ABIDE-derived secondary/validation cohort: 58 ASD, 51 TD, matched by age/sex/IQ.
narrative_rows.methods: Both cohorts preprocessed identically with fMRIPrep v1.3.1; FD-based scrubbing (>0.5mm) and <80% TR-retention exclusion; whole-thalamus seed-based whole-brain GLM connectivity with site as a covariate in the ABIDE analysis; Bonferroni correction for five seeds.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Right thalamus hyperconnectivity with right precentral/postcentral gyri in ASD vs TD replicated in the ABIDE cohort (p=0.019, p=0.028), supporting thalamocortical hyperconnectivity in high-functioning adult ASD.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: ABIDE selection process detailed only in an unretrieved supplement; diagnosis source for ABIDE subset not independently restated; whole-thalamus (not nuclei-specific) seeds used due to low-resolution imaging.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Demonstrates use of ABIDE as an independent validation cohort for an associational finding originating in a non-ABIDE sample, with explicit site-covariate handling and motion QC thresholds applied to the ABIDE subset.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Group-difference (associational) voxel-wise R-fMRI study; ABIDE I+II discovery sample, N=1019 (82 F ASD, 362 M ASD, 166 NT F, 409 NT M) across 13 merged sites; replicated in EU-AIMS LEAP and GENDAAR.
narrative_rows.methods: Custom R-fMRI preprocessing (slice-timing, motion regression, CompCor, band-pass filter, BBR+ANTs registration) with ComBat site harmonisation; five metrics (PCC-iFC, VMHC, ReHo, DC, fALFF) analysed via voxel-wise GLM with diagnosis, sex and their interaction as regressors, age and mFD as covariates.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Main effects of diagnosis and sex converged on the default-network midline across PCC-iFC, ReHo and VMHC; a sex-by-diagnosis interaction on VMHC in dorsolateral occipital cortex (reduced VMHC in autistic females) replicated in EU-AIMS LEAP but not GENDAAR.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: Lack of a priori harmonisation among discovery and replication datasets; diagnosis-confirmation method not restated in main text; replicability varied by metric and sample.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Large, methodologically transparent use of combined ABIDE I+II data with explicit QC thresholds, ComBat site harmonisation, and independent-sample replication — a strong example of reconstructible cohort definition.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Diagnostic prediction study; ABIDE I+II, final N=297 (151 ASD, 146 TD) from 4 sites (NYU, PITT, USM, TCD), reduced to N=290 (145/145) after propensity-score matching on age, sex and site.
narrative_rows.methods: Rs-fMRI preprocessed with C-PAC (Preprocessed Connectomes Project); functional connectivity via a 100-region Schaefer-Yeo atlas; ASD vs TD classification under contiguous/diverse/random training-stratum sampling schemes with 10-fold CV, evaluated within- and out-of-distribution; linear-regression and ComBat deconfounding tested.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Prediction accuracy (AUC, F1) and extracted-pattern stability declined as participant diversity increased in ABIDE (opposite direction to HBN); deconfounding only partially reduced this diversity-performance relationship.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: Propensity-score and deconfounding computations used the full sample rather than training-fold-only data, a leakage concern flagged by the authors; negligible female representation in ABIDE (<0.02%) limited sex-related analysis.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Directly interrogates how ABIDE's site/demographic composition (diversity) affects reproducibility of predictive findings; open code and data make the analysed cohort reconstructible; illustrates a leakage pattern (full-sample deconfounding) relevant to RQ4/CL5 across the corpus.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Group-difference (associational) discovery + independent validation; ABIDE I discovery N=708 (432 TD, 276 ASD), ABIDE II validation N=585 (316 TD, 269 ASD, 11 sites).
narrative_rows.methods: Athena-pipeline-preprocessed rs-fMRI; FD-based motion scrubbing with >5%-removed exclusion rule; cortico-cerebellar connectivity via linear regression of 65 cortical ROIs against cerebellar PCs, with site as a covariate; FDR correction across tests.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Five ROIs showed reduced (hypo-) cortico-cerebellar connectivity in ASD in ABIDE I; three (right fusiform gyrus, right superior temporal gyrus, left middle temporal gyrus) replicated in the independent ABIDE II sample.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: Incomplete cerebellar coverage in some individuals (particularly posterior cerebellum); diagnosis-source instrument not independently restated; no atlas-based parcellation named.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: A clean discovery/validation example using both ABIDE I and ABIDE II with transparent QC and site-covariate handling, illustrating cross-release replication of an associational finding.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Diagnostic prediction (deep ensemble); ABIDE I CPAC data, N=1035 (505 ASD, 530 TC) from 17 sites; NYU subset N=175 (78 ASD, 104 TC); self-selected 'proposed subset' N=645.
narrative_rows.methods: Functional connectivity computed via CPAC pipeline across three atlases (AAL, CC200, EZ), F-score feature selection, and a stacked sparse denoising autoencoder + MLP ensemble with demographic features, fused by weighted voting; evaluated with 10-fold cross-validation.
narrative_rows.outcomes: 75.20% accuracy on the whole ABIDE I dataset (SOTA, +4.4 points over prior best); 88.71% on a selector-defined 'proposed subset'; 96.40% on the NYU site subset.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: F-score feature selection described as using the whole dataset rather than training folds only; the 'proposed subset' is defined by the selector model's own correct classifications, a circularity that inflates its reported accuracy; no site harmonisation or leave-site-out evaluation; diagnosis-source instrument not independently restated.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: A fully reproducible (code-released), multi-atlas ABIDE I predictive study illustrating both best practice (open code, multiple atlases, demographic fusion) and a clear leakage pattern (selector-defined subset) relevant to the review's Analysis-domain checklist.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Diagnostic prediction / methodological tutorial; ABIDE, N=154 (77 ASD, 77 TD), balanced and matched per site.
narrative_rows.methods: SPM12/DARTEL-preprocessed rs-fMRI; 200-ROI Craddock-atlas connectivity (19,900 features); six classifiers (LR, LassoLR, SVM, PNN, LDA, GNB) compared via nested 10x10-fold cross-validation with train-only feature selection and standardization.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Best out-of-the-box accuracy 63% (linear SVM), improving to 68% with per-site train-only standardization; a simulation shows incorrect whole-dataset feature selection can inflate accuracy to 91%, illustrating the 'peeking'/double-dipping pitfall.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: Diagnosis-source instrument not independently restated; leave-one-site-out CV discussed but not reported as the authors' own executed analysis; relatively modest sample size (N=154).
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: A rare positive methodological exemplar in this corpus: explicitly demonstrates and guards against the leakage patterns (whole-dataset feature selection/standardization) that affect several other ABIDE predictive papers in this review.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Diagnostic prediction (MHPC ensemble); ABIDE, N=1111 (573 controls, 538 ASD) from 17 institutions, split into 889 training / 222 hold-out test subjects.
narrative_rows.methods: SPM8-based preprocessing; 3D-HOG voxel-texture features from functional and/or structural MRI combined with personal characteristic data; MRMR feature selection and classifier/hyperparameter tuning via training-set cross-validation; single evaluation on a held-out test set.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Best ABIDE accuracy 65.0% (functional MRI + personal characteristics) vs 51.6% baseline, exceeding functional MRI alone (59.2%), structural MRI alone (60.1%) and PCD alone (59.6%).
narrative_rows.key_limitations: No connectivity atlas/parcellation used; site of imaging used as a raw feature rather than harmonised; no specific motion-metric threshold reported.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: A clear example of hold-out-set discipline (feature selection/tuning strictly on training data) for ABIDE predictive modelling, though site handling via raw feature inclusion is methodologically distinct from harmonisation or leave-site-out approaches used elsewhere in this corpus.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Group-difference (associational) voxel-wise analysis; ABIDE I, N=975 (458 ASD, 517 TDC) after site/IQ/coverage-based exclusions from 1112 raw datasets.
narrative_rows.methods: SPM8-preprocessed rs-fMRI; whole-brain voxel-wise functional connectivity density (global, inter-hemispheric/contralateral, intra-hemispheric/ipsilateral) with a 2-tailed t-test (age, sex covariates), FDR-corrected P<0.05, 20-voxel minimum cluster size.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Decreased inter- and intra-hemispheric FCD in ASD vs TDC in posterior cingulate cortex, lingual/parahippocampal gyrus, and postcentral gyrus; ADOS-RRB negatively correlated with FCD in these and default-mode-network regions.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: No motion-based subject-exclusion threshold reported; no site covariate or harmonisation despite pooling multiple sites; no atlas-based parcellation.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: A voxel-wise (non-atlas) associational use of ABIDE I illustrating a common gap in this corpus: multi-site pooling without explicit site-effect statistical handling.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Group-difference (associational) study; original non-ABIDE cohort (21 ASD/24 TD, Japan) plus an ABIDE II replication cohort of 42 ASD / 88 TD boys drawn from 5 sites (GU, KKI, NYU_1, NYU_2 [excluded], SDSU)
narrative_rows.methods: Seed-based ROI-to-ROI resting-state functional connectivity from cerebellar subregions (Diedrichsen probabilistic atlas) to cerebral cortex, using CONN toolbox/SPM12 preprocessing; two-sample t-tests with FD, FSIQ and site as covariates, FDR-corrected (original) / Bonferroni-corrected (replication) thresholds
narrative_rows.outcomes: 12 cerebellar-cerebral FC group differences found in the original dataset (mixed increased/decreased); one (right dentate nucleus-left IPL decreased FC, p=0.039) replicated significantly in ABIDE II; FC values correlated with motor, executive and socio-communicative measures in the original dataset
narrative_rows.key_limitations: Small original sample; only partial replication in ABIDE II (1/12 findings surviving correction); no code or participant-list release found
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Demonstrates use of a specific ABIDE II site/criteria subset purely as an independent replication sample for an externally-derived finding, with exact numeric selection rules reported.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Diagnostic prediction study; ABIDE I, 1035 subjects (505 ASD, 530 HC), pooled across all contributing sites
narrative_rows.methods: CPAC-preprocessed resting-state functional connectivity (Harvard-Oxford atlas, 110 ROIs) classified with a novel graph attention network (GAT2) within a graph-learning-and-interpreting framework (GAT-LI); compared against SVM, RF, MLP, CNN and other GNN baselines using fivefold cross-validation
narrative_rows.outcomes: GAT2 achieved the best classification performance among compared models (accuracy 68.02%, sensitivity 74.06%, F1 69.31%, MCC 0.3426 with the HO atlas); GNNExplainer-based interpretation identified a set of discriminative functional connections, 3 of which showed uncorrected group differences (p<0.05)
narrative_rows.key_limitations: No leave-site-out or site-covariate evaluation despite multi-site data; no motion/QC rule reported for the analysed subset; post-hoc connection-level tests uncorrected for multiple comparisons
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Full ABIDE I 1035-subject PCP release used with CPAC/HO atlas; code and data source publicly linked, supporting reconstructibility of the pipeline though not an explicit subject-selection rule.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Diagnostic prediction study; ABIDE I, NYU site only, 184 subjects (79 ASD, 105 TC)
narrative_rows.methods: CCS-preprocessed (filt_global) resting-state fMRI 3D volumes converted into 2D slice images, classified with a modified Darknet-19 CNN (DarkASDNet)
narrative_rows.outcomes: DarkASDNet achieved accuracy 94.7%, precision 94.5%, recall 92.5%, F1-score 95%, AUC 94.703%, reported as outperforming VGG16, MobileNetV2, SVM and several literature benchmarks on the NYU subset
narrative_rows.key_limitations: No train/test split or cross-validation methodology described; single-site analysis limits generalisability; data available only on author request, no code repository found
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Single-site (NYU) ABIDE-I subset with an explicit N and phenotype table, but the prediction pipeline lacks a stated validation scheme, limiting confidence in the reported accuracy.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Diagnostic prediction study; ABIDE-I single-site cohorts (NYU 184, UM 110 subjects) and a multi-site cohort (19 sites, 1100 subjects)
narrative_rows.methods: C-PAC-preprocessed raw 4D resting-state fMRI volumes (4mm MNI) classified end-to-end with a hybrid 3D CNN + bidirectional 3D convolutional LSTM, evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation and compared against several published deep-learning ABIDE classifiers
narrative_rows.outcomes: 3DCNN C-LSTM achieved state-of-the-art single-site performance (NYU F1 0.78, UM F1 0.70), surpassing prior methods by 8-10%, but performance degraded substantially on the pooled multi-site ABIDE-I evaluation (F1 0.53), attributed to scanner/acquisition heterogeneity
narrative_rows.key_limitations: No leave-site-out evaluation despite multi-site heterogeneity being identified as the cause of degraded performance; no motion/QC rule or diagnostic-instrument description reported; no code or data-availability statement
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Illustrates that an end-to-end raw-4D-volume classifier that performs well at single sites degrades sharply under multi-site heterogeneity when evaluated with ordinary (non-site-stratified) cross-validation.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Diagnostic prediction study; ABIDE I single-site cohorts, NYU (184 subjects: 79 ASD, 105 NC, primary) and UM (secondary)
narrative_rows.methods: DPARSF-preprocessed resting-state fMRI, multi-scale functional connectivity networks built from AAL (116 ROIs) and CC200 (200 ROIs) atlases, classified with a multi-scale graph convolutional network (MGRL) with feature fusion; evaluated with a repeated random 80/10/10 split (100 repeats)
narrative_rows.outcomes: MGRL outperformed single-scale GCN and handcrafted-feature baselines on both sites (NYU accuracy 0.795, AUC 0.886; UM accuracy 0.762, AUC 0.867), with multi-scale atlas fusion improving performance by at least 3% over single-atlas GCNs
narrative_rows.key_limitations: Restricted to single sites to avoid inter-site heterogeneity rather than modelling it; no leave-site-out or pooled multi-site evaluation; diagnostic instrument/criteria and motion QC threshold not described; data availability limited to a general statement with no code link
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Demonstrates an atlas-fusion GCN approach validated with a repeated-split uncertainty estimate on two separate ABIDE single-site subsets, explicitly avoiding rather than addressing multi-site heterogeneity.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Diagnostic prediction study; two ABIDE I-derived multimodal benchmarks, ABIDE A (871 subjects: 403 ASD, 468 TC) and ABIDE B (949 subjects: 419 ASD, 530 TC)
narrative_rows.methods: C-PAC-preprocessed resting-state fMRI connectivity (CC200/AAL/Dosenbach160 atlases) combined with phenotypic and QC modalities, classified with a multimodal adversarial-regularized graph learning model (DeepASD) using patient similarity graphs and a GNN classifier; evaluated with 10-fold stratified, non-overlapping cross-validation
narrative_rows.outcomes: DeepASD outperformed 8 state-of-the-art baselines (accuracy 87.38% / AUC 92.76% on ABIDE A; accuracy 88.09% / AUC 93.59% on ABIDE B), an improvement of 13.25% accuracy, 7.69% AUC-ROC and 17.10% specificity over the best baseline; ablation confirmed fMRI as the most informative single modality, with other modalities adding further gains
narrative_rows.key_limitations: Diagnostic label source/instrument not elaborated; site is incorporated as a demographic feature for graph construction rather than evaluated with a leave-site-out scheme despite the known multi-site heterogeneity of ABIDE
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Both cohorts are explicitly reconstructible by citation to previously published preprocessing protocols (Parisot 2017, Wang 2020), and both preprocessed datasets plus analysis code are released with the paper.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Diagnostic prediction study; ABIDE I, 880 subjects (418 ASD, 478 TD) across 17 sites after excluding incomplete/missing data
narrative_rows.methods: CPAC-preprocessed resting-state functional connectivity (Harvard-Oxford atlas, 110 ROIs) used to learn non-linear high-order functional associations via an explainability-guided ROI-selection stacked-autoencoder framework (EAG-RS), evaluated with stratified five-fold cross-validation
narrative_rows.outcomes: EAG-RS achieved AUC 0.760, accuracy 73.71%, sensitivity 64.56%, specificity 80.74%, outperforming comparative state-of-the-art and feature-selection methods; selected ROIs were linked to previously reported ASD-relevant brain regions and subtypes
narrative_rows.key_limitations: No site covariate, harmonisation, or leave-site-out evaluation despite the pooled 17-site cohort; diagnostic instrument/criteria not elaborated; the paper itself notes it does not incorporate other neuroimaging modalities or clinical information
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Exact exclusion rule, pipeline, atlas and analysis code (GitHub) are all reported, supporting reconstructibility of the analysed cohort from the released ABIDE I data.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Diagnostic prediction study; ABIDE I, 406 ASD and 476 TC subjects (DPARSF-preprocessed PCP subset) across 17 sites
narrative_rows.methods: DPARSF-preprocessed resting-state fMRI connectivity from three atlases (AAL, CC200, Dosenbach160) classified with a multi-atlas transformer (METAFormer) using self-supervised masked-value pretraining, evaluated with 10-fold stratified cross-validation and a separate validation split per fold
narrative_rows.outcomes: Pretrained METAFormer achieved accuracy 83.7%, AUC 0.832, outperforming non-pretrained and single-atlas variants as well as previously published ABIDE I classifiers using comparable cross-validation
narrative_rows.key_limitations: No explanation given for the reduction from the full 1112-subject ABIDE I release to the 406/476 analysed subset; no site covariate, harmonisation, or leave-site-out evaluation despite the pooled 17-site cohort; diagnostic instrument/criteria not elaborated
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Pipeline, atlases and analysis code (GitHub) are all reported, and the leakage-aware CV design (separate validation fold) is an explicit methodological strength noted in the paper itself.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Group-difference (associational) / methods-comparison study; ABIDE I, 850 subjects (355 ASD, 495 HC) from multiple sites
narrative_rows.methods: CCS-preprocessed resting-state functional connectivity (CC200 atlas, Fisher z-transformed), compared across three site-effect mitigation strategies (GLM, ComBat, and the proposed site-wise de-meaning) using Hedge's g effect size on a literature-anchored ASD finding (anterior-posterior DMN hypoconnectivity)
narrative_rows.outcomes: Site-wise de-meaning (SWD) improved ASD-vs-control effect size by 2.9-5.3% relative to uncorrected data, while GLM and ComBat reduced it by up to 11.4% and 7.5% respectively, indicating SWD better preserves disorder-related connectivity signal under multi-site harmonisation
narrative_rows.key_limitations: Evaluation restricted to specific literature-selected ROI pairs rather than a whole-brain corrected analysis; no code repository identified beyond the public ABIDE data link
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Directly addresses RQ on site handling (CL6) with a quantitative comparison of three site-effect mitigation strategies applied to ABIDE I resting-state connectivity.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Diagnostic prediction (3D CNN) using ABIDE-I (10-fold CV training set, n=774: 379 ASD/395 TD, 17 sites) and ABIDE-II (independent held-out test, n=393: 163 ASD/230 TD, sites overlapping ABIDE-I).
narrative_rows.methods: CPAC/PCP-preprocessed connectivity fingerprints across seven atlases fed into a volumetric 3D CNN; compared against ridge regression, linear SVM, and fully-connected DNN baselines; evaluated via 10-fold CV on ABIDE-I and an independent held-out test on ABIDE-II.
narrative_rows.outcomes: 3D-CNN atlas-ensemble reached 73.3% CV accuracy (ABIDE-I) and 71.7% independent test accuracy (ABIDE-II), AUC 75.8% on the ABIDE-II test, outperforming all baselines and a prior ABIDE-I benchmark of up to 67%.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: No code/participant-list availability statement; baseline hyperparameters tuned by maximising CV accuracy (acknowledged optimistic); no explicit site covariate/harmonisation; ABIDE-II test sites overlap with ABIDE-I training sites rather than being fully held out; diagnostic label source not described.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Demonstrates volumetric 3D-CNN classification with atlas-ensemble voting, trained on ABIDE-I and externally validated on an independent ABIDE-II cohort; a cross-release external-validation example linking the two ABIDE phases.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Diagnostic prediction trained on the IMPAC dataset (n=915) and externally validated on ABIDE I (n=1045, all sites) and ABIDE II (n=761, all sites), restricted to subjects with a paired same-visit sMRI+rsfMRI scan.
narrative_rows.methods: fconn1000-derived functional connectivity (tangent-space embedding across seven atlases) plus FreeSurfer structural features; 12 ML model types trained/optimised on IMPAC only; ABIDE I/II used as untouched external test sets, with a secondary supervised-domain-adaptation analysis (10-fold CV).
narrative_rows.outcomes: Best IMPAC model: 80.4% AUROC (IMPAC); 86.0% AUROC (ABIDE I) and 79.2% AUROC (ABIDE II) without adaptation; 93.2%/90.5% after supervised domain adaptation. Cerebellar connectivity identified as a reproducible discriminative feature.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: Exact per-diagnosis Ns for ABIDE are not reported (percentages only); no motion/QC rule or site harmonisation reported for the ABIDE external-validation cohort; diagnostic label source not described.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: A strong example of cross-dataset external validation (IMPAC-trained, ABIDE-tested) with openly released code, pipeline and model weights, directly linking the ABIDE releases to an independently trained predictive model.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Diagnostic prediction (federated learning) using ABIDE I resting-state fMRI from four sites: NYU (n=167: 73 ASD/94 HC), UM1 (n=88: 43/45), USM (n=52: 33/19), UCLA1 (n=63: 37/26).
narrative_rows.methods: CPAC-preprocessed ROI time series (Harvard-Oxford atlas, 0.01-0.1Hz band-pass, no GSR; CC200 atlas as replication) fed into MLP classifiers trained under a privacy-preserving federated-learning framework, with two domain-adaptation extensions (MoE, adversarial alignment); compared against single-site, cross-site, ensemble and pooled (Mix) training via 5-fold CV.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Federated learning (Fed) outperformed single-site and best cross-site training at every site (accuracy 0.647-0.849 across sites, HO atlas) and approached pooled (Mix) accuracy without centralising data; domain adaptation further improved accuracy at most sites; results replicated (at lower absolute accuracy) with the CC200 atlas.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: No motion/FD-based QC rule or statistical site harmonisation (e.g. ComBat) reported; diagnostic label source not described; no code/participant-list availability statement; class balance (ASD%) varies by site (44-63%) without an explicit correction.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Demonstrates that privacy-preserving federated learning across four ABIDE I sites can approach the accuracy of pooled multi-site training without data sharing, directly relevant to the dataset's distributed, multi-site structure.
